newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan allows Sinopac to buy China-linked US bank.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan allows Sinopac to buy China-linked US bank.

text.p: Taiwan's Finance Ministry said on Monday it had approved Bank Sinopac's purchase of Far East National Bank despite "complications" arising from the California target bank's operations in communist China.
Finance Minister Paul Chiu told reporters that the Taiwan bank's US$80 million takeover of Far East National had been approved after thorough, eight-month interagency review.

Because Far East National has an office in the communist Chinese mainland, Taiwan's arch rival, the acquisition had to be approved by Taipei's Mainland Affairs Council, a cabinet agency that oversees such sensitive Taiwan-China issues, Chiu said.

"Since it's an established fact that the bank (Far East National) has an office in Beijing, it doesn't really violate our policy," Chiu said. "Furthermore, that bank doesn't have any business activities (in China) so the council approved."

Chiu said that because of the political "complications" surrounding Bank Sinopac's proposed acquisition, his ministry's approval should be viewed as an individual case, not a precedent for other Taiwan banks eyeing mainland investments.
Deeply wary of becoming overdependent on the economy of its longtime rival, Taiwan explicitly bans investment by local interests in mainland banks and other financial institutions.

Chiu's brief comments to reporters made clear that Taipei did not regard Far East National's Beijing office as a financial institution since it operates only as a liaison office and does not take deposits or make loans.
Only a few dozen western banks are allowed to operate branches in China, of which a handful only recently were granted the right to do local-currency business.

Bank Sinopac said it had given a vow to Taiwan's Finance Ministry that it would not grow the Beijing office without the ministry's approval -- and would even shut it down if recently strained Taiwan-China relations soured further.
"If conditions across the Taiwan strait were to worsen, we would close the Beijing office," a Bank Sinopac spokeswoman told Reuters by telephone.

Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, but a late-1980s thaw in their once-icy relations has allowed economic ties to flourish, with Taiwan firms investing some US$30 billion in the mainland.

Bank Sinopac 5814.TWO, listed in Taiwan's over-the-counter market, has made a local splash in with its technological and marketing savvy, quickly growing a 27-branch Taiwan network with assets of T$120 billion since its establishment in 1992.

The Far East National takeover gives it a U.S. foothold and a push toward its goal of becoming a "trans-Pacific" bank with operations in Hong Kong, Singapore, Indonesia, Vietnam and other Pacific markets, Bank Sinopac executives have said.

Executives said they hoped to grow potentially lucrative banking ties between the pre-eminent U.S. high-technology centre, California's Silicon Valley, and Taiwan's flourishing Hsinchu Science Park, where the merged banks have offices.

Far East National, with 10 branches in southern California and the San Francisco Bay Area and net assets of US$44 million, has averaged after-tax net profits of 15 percent over the past five years, executives have said.
Far East National will retain its name after the takeover.
